newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Greenpeace protests in NZ over plutonium ship.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace protests in NZ over plutonium ship.

text.p: Greenpeace activists protested outside the Japanese consulate in Auckland on Wednesday and New Zealand expressed regret at news that a ship carrying plutonium waste to Japan would pass through the southwest Pacific.
About 20 Greenpeace protesters demonstrated outside the consulate while climbers unfurled a banner reading "New Zealanders say no to plutonium" on the building.

Foreign Minister Don McKinnon said he was "extremely disappointed" that the British ship Pacific Teal, carrying processed nuclear waste, would transit the South Pacific on its way from France to Japan.

"We made it clear to Japan, and to the other countries involved in the shipment, that New Zealand did not want it to come anywhere near us. Despite our representations, and those of other South Pacific countries, the vessel will be passing through our region," he said.
"The Japanese government can be under no illusion that it will do so against the wishes of the people of the South Pacific."
Greenpeace called on McKinnon to go further.
The waste orginally came from Japan and was processed by French state company COGEMA, which released sketchy details of the ship's route on Tuesday.

New Zealand, braving U.S. anger, passed legislation in the mid-1980s banning nuclear-powered and nuclear-armed ships from its waters. It forms part of a self-declared nuclear-free zone in the South Pacific.

Wellington says it cannot legally prevent the ship from sailing through the Tasman Sea, which separates New Zealand and Australia. But McKinnon again called for it to stay out of New Zealand's 200-mile (320 km) economic zone.
"He doesn't need to convince the New Zealand public that he's disappointed, he needs to call in the (Japanese) ambassador to tell him that this is outrageous," spokeswoman Stephanie Mills said.

She said it was uncertain under international law which country would be responsible for any accident involving the nuclear waste shipment, and New Zealand should urge Japan to accept full liability in the event of any damage.
"If Japan is acting in good faith and is confident in the safety of its cargo, there's no reason why it shouldn't give an assurance of total liability," she said.

The opposition Labour party challenged the government to mobilise a strong diplomatic reaction from Australia and other South Pacific nations against the "hideously dangerous trade" in nuclear waste. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
